Houttuynia cordata 'Chameleon' is a colorful variegated sport of the East Asian herb prized in Vietnamese and Chinese cooking for its citrus-and-fish-scented leaves, with heart-shaped foliage splashed in red, cream, yellow, and green and small white flower bracts in summer. The leaves are edible with the same distinctive pungent, coriander-and-citrus flavor as the plain green species and are used fresh in salads and wraps, but the cultivar is grown mainly as a striking, tough groundcover for wet shade, pond margins, and rain gardens where its color and vigor are assets rather than liabilities. Because it spreads so readily by rhizome and is difficult to fully eradicate once established, confine it firmly to containers or barrier-lined beds away from more delicate neighbors.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost and transplant out 1–3 weeks after the last frost once soil has warmed in full sun; Malagueta pepper is a heavy-yielding, upright frutescens type similar to tabasco pepper that continues producing through summer heat.

Capsicum frutescens 'Malagueta' is the iconic hot pepper of Brazilian cuisine, prized for the tangy, piri-piri-style hot sauce and pepper-infused vinegar (molho de pimenta) served at Brazilian steakhouses, producing prolific clusters of small, slender, upward-pointing fruit that ripen from green through yellow-orange to red with intense, sharp heat around 60,000–100,000 Scoville units. Plants form a bushy, productive shrub over the growing season and, like other frutescens peppers, tolerate heat and humidity well, making them reliable producers through the hottest part of a Gulf Coast summer. In frost-free zones plants can be overwintered as a short-lived perennial shrub; elsewhere grow as a warm-season annual and harvest continuously to encourage further fruit set.
sources: Chile Pepper Institute (New Mexico State University)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give 'Gigantea' extra room compared with standard leopard plant, since its leaves grow considerably larger and the clump spreads wider at maturity.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; give 'Gigantea' extra room compared with standard leopard plant, since its leaves grow considerably larger and the clump spreads wider at maturity. This selection of leopard plant produces dramatically oversized, glossy, rounded leaves nearly twice the size of the species, creating a bold, tropical-textured mass in a shaded border, bog garden, or large container where a strong architectural statement is wanted. Clusters of daisy-like yellow flowers rise above the foliage on tall stalks in fall, adding late-season color after most other shade perennials have finished blooming. Give it consistently moist soil, since the outsized leaves wilt dramatically in dry conditions, and protect from hard freezes and drying winter wind where marginally hardy.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; like all ligularia, 'Britt-Marie Crawford' wilts dramatically in afternoon sun or dry soil even when the root zone is otherwise healthy, so site it in a reliably damp, sheltered spot.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in constantly moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; like all ligularia, 'Britt-Marie Crawford' wilts dramatically in afternoon sun or dry soil even when the root zone is otherwise healthy, so site it in a reliably damp, sheltered spot. This striking Ligularia dentata selection pairs the species' large, rounded leaves with deep chocolate-purple-black foliage color that persists through the season, topped in mid to late summer by clusters of vivid orange-yellow, daisy-like flowers that contrast dramatically with the dark leaves. It is one of the most popular ornamental ligularia cultivars for its combination of bold dark foliage and bright bloom, making a strong focal point at a pond edge, rain garden, or the moist, shaded portion of a mixed border. Consistent moisture is essential — plants sited in anything less than reliably damp soil will scorch and wilt in summer heat regardless of how much shade they receive.

planting.note: Broadcast seed in spring once soil has warmed, or plant plugs, into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; dichondra tolerates foot traffic and mowing far better than most shade groundcovers, making it a genuine turfgrass alternative for lawns under trees.

directions: Broadcast seed in spring once soil has warmed, or plant plugs, into well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; dichondra tolerates foot traffic and mowing far better than most shade groundcovers, making it a genuine turfgrass alternative for lawns under trees. Dichondra micrantha is a low, mat-forming perennial with small, rounded, bright green, kidney-shaped leaves that has long been used across the warm-climate South and California as a fine-textured lawn substitute in shaded areas where turfgrass thins out, spreading by creeping stems that root at the nodes to knit into a dense, weed-suppressing carpet. It tolerates regular mowing to keep it low and neat, handles moderate foot traffic, and stays green through the warm season with regular water, though it goes off-color and semi-dormant with cold snaps in the cooler part of its range. It needs reasonably good drainage and a warm climate to thrive, struggling in prolonged freezes or waterlogged, poorly drained soil.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources
